issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, is justified in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the trial court and the first appellate court?

facts: The trial court and the first appellate court both convicted the respondent for offenses under the Drugs and Cosmetics Act.
These two lower courts reached a "concurrent finding of fact" that the respondent was guilty based on the evidence presented.
In a revision petition, the High Court reversed the conviction and acquitted the respondent.
The High Court's reasons for acquittal included the non-examination of the shop's previous owner and the claim that the respondent's signatures were obtained on blank papers.
law: The Supreme Court established that a High Court's revisional jurisdiction is different from and more limited than its appellate jurisdiction.
A High Court should not normally interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by lower courts.
Interference is only permissible in exceptional cases, such as when the lower courts' findings are "perverse" or when they have ignored material evidence.

Citing *State of Kerala v. Puttumana Illath Jathavedan Namboodiri*, the Court affirmed that it is not appropriate for a High Court in revision to reappreciate the evidence and arrive at its own conclusion.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court had improperly re-appreciated the evidence, which both the trial court and the first appellate court had already considered.

The lower courts had already determined that the non-examination of the previous owner was not fatal to the prosecution's case, especially since the respondent admitted to owning the shop and not having a license.
The Supreme Court dismissed the respondent's claim about signing blank papers as an "afterthought," noting the lack of any prior complaint to the police or higher authorities.
Since the findings of the lower courts were not perverse and did not ignore material evidence, the High Court had no valid reason to interfere.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact of the trial court and the first appellate court. By re-appreciating the evidence, the High Court exceeded the limited scope of its revisional jurisdiction, and therefore its order acquitting the respondent could not be sustained.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court, in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, is justified in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact recorded by the trial court and the first appellate court?
appellant_arguments: The appellant's argument, as supported by the court's reasoning, is that the High Court should not interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by the lower courts while exercising its revisional jurisdiction. This jurisdiction is limited and does not permit a re-appreciation of evidence unless the findings are perverse or have ignored material evidence.
respondent_arguments: The prosecution failed to prove that the respondent was the owner of M/s Sri Balaji Medicals.
The non-examination of key witnesses, Kamalakannan and Jayanthi, was fatal to the prosecution's case.
The lower courts should not have based the conviction on the respondent's statements (Exs.P-4, P-7 and P-10) as they were only carbon copies.
The respondent's signatures were obtained on blank papers, which were then used to create the incriminating exhibits (Exs.P-4, P-7 and P-10).

cases.case_name: State of Kerala v. Puttumana Illath Jathavedan Namboodiri
cases.principle: Ordinarily, it is not appropriate for the High Court in its revisional jurisdiction to reappreciate evidence and come to its own conclusion when the evidence has already been appreciated by the Magistrate and the Sessions court in appeal, especially in cases of concurrent findings of fact.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A High Court, in the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, shall not interfere with concurrent findings of fact recorded by lower courts unless those findings are perverse or have been reached by ignoring material evidence. It is inappropriate for a High Court in revision to reappreciate evidence that has already been considered by both the trial court and the first appellate court.
obiter: The revisional jurisdiction of the High Court is different from the appellate jurisdiction.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When there is concurrent findings by the courts below, the High Court ought not to have interfered with the same in exercise of its revisional jurisdiction. When the courts below recorded the concurrent findings of fact, the High Court was not right in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact arrived at by the courts below and the impugned order cannot be sustained.
legal_tests_applied: The revisional jurisdiction of the High Court is different from the appellate jurisdiction. The High court will not normally interfere with the concurrent findings of fact, unless the findings of fact arrived at by the courts below is perverse or that the court has ignored the material evidence while arriving at that finding.

Ordinarily it would not be appropriate for the High Court to reappreciate the evidence and come to its own conclusion on the same when the evidence has already been appreciated by the Magistrate as well as by the Sessions court in appeal.
why_respondent_won: While the respondent's conviction was affirmed, the sentence was reduced because the court invoked the proviso to Section 27(b)(ii) of the Act for 'adequate and special reasons', which were: the offence was committed ten years back, the respondent had no prior conviction under the Act, and the respondent had stated in his statement that he was not aware that he had to obtain a licence for the sale of drugs.
policy_considerations: The Drugs and Cosmetics Act, 1940 is a social statute which provides for checks and balances so that drugs are sold strictly only by the licence-holder or that the adulterated drugs are not sold.
Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, in the interest of justice, the proviso to Section 27(b)(ii) of the Act can be invoked to reduce the sentence.
